There are times when free choice isn't all it's cracked up to be. Just ask anyone who has recently signed up for a new mobile phone plan, internet service package, bank account or health insurance policy.
The idea that we're going to have to go through the same complexity to decide where to invest our super is, for many people, more of a headache than a liberation.
But take a hint from the 30 per cent of employees who already have the right to choose where to put their super. Unless you have a burning desire to select your own investments, keep it simple. And, in many cases, there may be no need to move from your existing fund.
While it's common to now see super offerings with hundreds - yes, hundreds - of different investment options, the bulk of super savings are still invested in traditional diversified or multi-sector funds. Even within funds that offer other investment options, the rule of thumb is that 90 per cent of fund members don't take advantage of those options. Instead, they remain with the default or standard offering.
And that's not solely due to ignorance or inertia.
One of the basic investment rules is that it pays to diversify your investments. Unless you're an absolute whiz in a particular investment sector, you're not going to be able to gauge exactly the right time to move in and out of each investment. You're also not going to have a 100 per cent strike rate on the investments you choose.
The unfortunate truth is that we're all fallible and no one investment is best over all parts of the investment cycle. By having a mix of investments, your returns will be smoothed out as good performance on some investments will make up for bad periods with others. (Though it is important to distinguish between a good investment that's going through a tough patch and a complete dud.)
A balanced or diversified fund can give you that smoother ride. While these funds can still lose money - and have done so several times recently - you shouldn't do your shirt. And over the long term, research company Intech reckons you can expect returns of around 4 per cent above the inflation rate for a growth-oriented fund (with 60 to 75 per cent of its money in growth assets) and 3 per cent above inflation for a slightly more conservative balanced fund (with 35 to 60 per cent in growth assets). On average, Intech estimates, the growth fund should have a negative return only one in every six years, while the balanced fund should lose money only once in every eight years.
While not all investors are comfortable with the idea of growth investments, the standard balanced or growth fund also fits the needs of the average fund member.
If you're investing for the long term - and for most of us, that's what retirement savings are all about - it just doesn't make sense to have all your money in conservative investments. Fixed-interest investments typically deliver several percentage points less in performance over the long term than growth investments. And when you're talking about retirement savings, a difference of a couple of percentage points a year can translate into tens of thousands of dollars.
If you're young and a reasonably aggressive investor, there's even an argument for having all your money in growth investments as you have more than enough time to ride out any dips in the market.
But for the majority of people, 50 to 60 per cent growth assets are a sensible trade-off between risk and long-term returns.
So the first thing to do, when it comes time to think about moving your super, is to have a closer look at what your existing fund is offering. If it is a sensibly structured diversified offering, has reasonable costs and has produced competitive returns over a reasonable period (five years is probably the minimum to consider), there's not much sense in being talked into moving just for the heck of it. Chances are the only person who will benefit will be the salesperson who gets the commission from your new fund.
As Phillipa Smith, the chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, puts it: "Look in the fridge before you go shopping."
Of course, there will be some investors who will benefit from choice. Investors who are forced by their employer to keep their money in poorly performing or expensive funds will have the opportunity to move to something better and cheaper. And, unlike personal super funds, investors in employer funds can generally move their money without being stung by big exit fees.
Some investors will also find that a different balanced fund may be better for their needs. For example, a younger person may choose to move to a more growth-oriented fund while someone nearing retirement might like to pull back their growth exposure a little.
More sophisticated investors who want to tailor their own super will also be able to use the full range of products - and options within products - available.

There are times when free choice isn't all it's cracked up to be. Just ask anyone who has recently signed up for a new mobile phone plan, internet service package, bank account or health insurance policy.
The idea that we're going to have to go through the same complexity to decide where to invest our super is, for many people, more of a headache than a liberation.
But take a hint from the 30 per cent of employees who already have the right to choose where to put their super. Unless you have a burning desire to select your own investments, keep it simple. And, in many cases, there may be no need to move from your existing fund.
While it's common to now see super offerings with hundreds - yes, hundreds - of different investment options, the bulk of super savings are still invested in traditional diversified or multi-sector funds. Even within funds that offer other investment options, the rule of thumb is that 90 per cent of fund members don't take advantage of those options. Instead, they remain with the default or standard offering.
And that's not solely due to ignorance or inertia.
One of the basic investment rules is that it pays to diversify your investments. Unless you're an absolute whiz in a particular investment sector, you're not going to be able to gauge exactly the right time to move in and out of each investment. You're also not going to have a 100 per cent strike rate on the investments you choose.
The unfortunate truth is that we're all fallible and no one investment is best over all parts of the investment cycle. By having a mix of investments, your returns will be smoothed out as good performance on some investments will make up for bad periods with others. (Though it is important to distinguish between a good investment that's going through a tough patch and a complete dud.)
A balanced or diversified fund can give you that smoother ride. While these funds can still lose money - and have done so several times recently - you shouldn't do your shirt. And over the long term, research company Intech reckons you can expect returns of around 4 per cent above the inflation rate for a growth-oriented fund (with 60 to 75 per cent of its money in growth assets) and 3 per cent above inflation for a slightly more conservative balanced fund (with 35 to 60 per cent in growth assets). On average, Intech estimates, the growth fund should have a negative return only one in every six years, while the balanced fund should lose money only once in every eight years.
While not all investors are comfortable with the idea of growth investments, the standard balanced or growth fund also fits the needs of the average fund member.
If you're investing for the long term - and for most of us, that's what retirement savings are all about - it just doesn't make sense to have all your money in conservative investments. Fixed-interest investments typically deliver several percentage points less in performance over the long term than growth investments. And when you're talking about retirement savings, a difference of a couple of percentage points a year can translate into tens of thousands of dollars.
If you're young and a reasonably aggressive investor, there's even an argument for having all your money in growth investments as you have more than enough time to ride out any dips in the market.
But for the majority of people, 50 to 60 per cent growth assets are a sensible trade-off between risk and long-term returns.
So the first thing to do, when it comes time to think about moving your super, is to have a closer look at what your existing fund is offering. If it is a sensibly structured diversified offering, has reasonable costs and has produced competitive returns over a reasonable period (five years is probably the minimum to consider), there's not much sense in being talked into moving just for the heck of it. Chances are the only person who will benefit will be the salesperson who gets the commission from your new fund.
As Phillipa Smith, the chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, puts it: "Look in the fridge before you go shopping."
Of course, there will be some investors who will benefit from choice. Investors who are forced by their employer to keep their money in poorly performing or expensive funds will have the opportunity to move to something better and cheaper. And, unlike personal super funds, investors in employer funds can generally move their money without being stung by big exit fees.
Some investors will also find that a different balanced fund may be better for their needs. For example, a younger person may choose to move to a more growth-oriented fund while someone nearing retirement might like to pull back their growth exposure a little.
More sophisticated investors who want to tailor their own super will also be able to use the full range of products - and options within products - available.
A balanced fund, with some risk, can provide good returns in a pinch. If you want to take on a huge number of risk-takers and have a balanced fund, then the balanced options portfolio may be worth examining.
But remember that any investment can be a fantastic investment for some - and risk-taking is a great thing. This article by Philipa Smith and Matt O'Shaughnessy was republished with permission from InvestorPlace.
